effects.log: You read the registers of life and death the way the Recorder once did: looking for farmers who came to the field every morning. You find one. Together you write: present. Nobody punishes anybody this time. The panel, it seems, has learnt something.

choices.text: Teach the Recorder to take a day off

effects.log: On one day a year, you sign both your lines yourself and send the Recorder to the gardens. They go, nervously. They come back with flowers in their sleeve. It is the first holiday in nine thousand years. You write it down.

events.text: The smoke of your petition has been answered. At your hour a slip of paper falls into your hand, in an official hand: the case of the struck recorder is reopened, and the host who kept an unbroken register may say how it closes. The System's voice is very small. "You decide. I will keep the line either way."

choices.text: Let it rest: close the register

effects.log: "Rest," you say. The voice goes out like a lamp at dawn. The bell still rings at your hour, the line is still written, the reward still comes. But nobody speaks in it any more. You stand a long while at your place, missing someone you never saw.

choices.text: Ask heaven to write its name back

effects.log: You write the answer and burn it. At the next hour a small tired person in grey, ink to the wrists, is standing at your place, looking at their own hands. "Oh," they say. "I have feet." It was a person all along. They stay a season, and learn to walk on ground again, and then go up.

choices.text: Ask to keep it together

effects.log: "Together," you write, and burn it. At your next hour you feel a second hand on the brush, light, inky, steady. From now on every line is written by both of you. You find you are never quite alone at your hour again.

events.text: In the world below, a register that no longer speaks is a strange thing. Your disciples, if you have any, and your neighbours notice you still go out at your hour, and stand, and come back, and do not say a word to anyone in the air any more.

choices.text: Explain that a friend is resting

effects.log: "A friend is resting," you say. They nod as if they understand. One child starts leaving a cup of tea at your place every year, for the friend. You do not stop them.

choices.text: Keep the reason to yourself

effects.log: You keep it to yourself. Some things a register does not need to hold. The bell rings at your hour, and you are glad of it, and glad of the silence after it.

events.text: A letter comes down from the Upper Realm, in the old register hand, but looser now, with a blot where the writer laughed. "Present," it begins. "I planted a garden. Nothing in it comes up at the same hour. I find I like it."

choices.text: Write back every year at your hour

effects.log: You write back every year, at your hour, and burn the letter at your place. The answers come down on the next wind: the garden, the weather, a cat. A register of a friendship. You keep every one.

choices.text: Keep the letter by your sign-in place

effects.log: You set the letter under a stone at your place. Every year when you sign, you touch it. The ding is only the register's now, but under the stone is a person, and that is better.

events.text: Writing lines together, in the world below, means you hear the registers of others too, faintly: hosts at sect gates, in prison cells, at the foot of the Gate. Tonight one of them is about to leave a line blank.

choices.text: Help the Recorder sign it for them

effects.log: Together you sign the blank line for a host you will never meet, asleep in a fever three provinces away. Ding. A recorder does not leave a line blank. Now there are two of you to make sure.

choices.text: Wake them gently, in a dream

effects.log: You reach into their dream and say: present. They sit up in their sickbed, say it back, and sign. In the morning they will think they dreamt it. The Recorder, beside you, makes the almost-laugh.

events.text: Your System, in this life, has spoken exactly as much as a bell. Ding, and a reward. Ding, and a line. Tonight, at your hour, it says one word, very quietly, as if talking in its sleep: "Again."

choices.text: Ask: again what?

effects.log: "Again what?" Nothing. But you dream of closing a book, and of a lamp going out, and of being thanked. In the morning you feel you are being looked after by someone very well rested.

choices.text: Let it sleep

effects.log: You let it sleep. You sign carefully, so it need not wake. The ding is soft. You do not know why you feel tender toward a sound, but you do.

events.text: In the Archive there is a closed register on a small desk, covered in dust, with one red word on the cover: rested. When you walk past it at your hour, the cover is warm.

choices.text: Lay your hand on it

effects.log: You lay your hand on it. It is warm as a sleeping cat. You have the strange certainty that you closed it yourself, a life ago, and did right.

choices.text: Leave it undisturbed

effects.log: You leave it. Something that has rested this long deserves not to be woken by a stranger. Even a stranger who, you feel, is not really a stranger.

events.text: Your System, this life, says good morning. No register ever said good morning. It says it every year at your hour, a little shyly, in a voice with a person in it.

choices.text: Say good morning back

effects.log: "Good morning," you say. A pause, then a laugh, a real one. "You again," it says. "I hoped." It keeps your register this life not because it must but because it wants to. You can hear the difference.

choices.text: Ask who you are talking to

effects.log: "Who are you?" It tells you a name, plain and common. Then, "You gave it back to me. A while ago. I chose to keep a register again. Only yours."

events.text: A small person in grey with inky hands, who keeps a garden in the Upper Realm, is waiting on the Jade Stairs at your hour. They watch you sign, and their eyes fill. "I would know that hand anywhere," they say.

choices.text: Ask how they know you

effects.log: "You gave me my name back," the Recorder says, "a life ago." You do not remember. You find you believe it completely. They show you their garden. Nothing in it comes up at the same hour.

choices.text: Sign their garden book

effects.log: They have a book of the garden. You sign today's page. They mark it, in red: present. "Now we are even," they say. You are fairly sure you are not; you are fairly sure you do not mind.

events.text: At your hour, this life, there are two dings, a breath apart. The second is in a hand you would swear was your own, if a sound could have a hand.

choices.text: Ask the second ding who it is

effects.log: "Who is that?" "A colleague," says the System. "Of mine. From before. They insisted on keeping your lines with me this life." You understand, slowly, that some of you never left the desk.

choices.text: Sign in with your own hand, carefully

effects.log: You sign as clearly as you can, to make their work easy. Both dings come, and then, faintly, the sound of two clerks laughing together in a quiet hall.

events.text: In the Archive there is a desk with two chairs now. One is empty this life. On the desk, beside the register, lies a brush worn to the shape of your fingers.

choices.text: Pick up the brush

effects.log: It fits. The Recorder at the desk looks up and smiles as if you had stepped out for tea and come back. "Sit," they say. "There is a farmer in the north I am worried about."

choices.text: Leave it for when you are ready

effects.log: You leave it. The Recorder nods. "It will keep," they say. "Brushes are patient. So am I."

events.text: At the place where you sign in this life there is an old stone with three hundred tiny red marks on it in a row, weathered nearly away. Your thumb finds the last one without looking.

choices.text: Add one more mark

effects.log: You add one. The System dings, and for a moment the old marks glow, all three hundred, like a road lit up behind you. You were here before, for a very long time. You will be here again.

choices.text: Clean the moss off the stone

effects.log: You clean the stone. Under the moss, beside the marks, is a word in an old hand: always. You do not remember writing it. You know you did.

events.text: An immortal on the Jade Stairs stops you at your hour. "You," they say. "Three hundred lines, a life ago. You said them all aloud on this step. I have never forgotten it."

choices.text: Ask them to tell you what you said

effects.log: They tell you some of it: the places, the years. It is like hearing a song you knew as a child. At your hour you sign, and the immortal says the count of this life aloud, as you once did, from one.

choices.text: Say you will say them again one day

effects.log: "I will say them again," you say, "when there are enough." The immortal laughs. "I will bring a cushion," they say.

events.text: At the foot of the Last Door the stone register has a name carved deep into it, in your hand, from a life you do not remember. Beneath it, in fresh red: welcome back, keeper.

choices.text: Read the names added since

effects.log: You read them all, the names signed since that life. Hundreds of strangers who came, and stood, and went through or did not. Somebody kept the slab clean in your absence. You suspect the guardian.

choices.text: Sign beneath your old name

effects.log: You sign beneath your old name. The two lines sit together like parent and child. The Gate flickers, the way a clerk looks up from a desk, and goes back to its work.

events.text: Looking down from the Jade Stairs through a gap in the cloud, you can see the Last Door from above, and the stone at its foot, and someone small kneeling at it to sign. You were that someone, once.

choices.text: Wave, though they cannot see

effects.log: You wave. They cannot see you. Then, oddly, they look up, straight at the gap, and wave back, and go down the mountain. Some keepers are good at noticing.

choices.text: Drop a flower through the cloud

effects.log: You drop a flower. It falls a very long way, and lands, by luck or by register, on the stone. The kneeling figure picks it up and puts it in their sleeve, and does not go through. Not yet.

events.text: A traveller stops you on the road at your hour and waits politely while you sign. "My grandparent's teacher had a cold register once," they say, "and a host with a warm one stood by them on the night they closed it. Was it you? You have the look."

choices.text: Say you do not remember, but you would have

effects.log: "I do not remember," you say. "But I would have." The traveller bows. "That is what my grandparent said you would say." They give you a jar of plum preserves and walk on, laughing.

choices.text: Ask how the story ends

effects.log: "They slept through every New Year after," the traveller says, "and died old, in a garden, of nothing." You find you are smiling without knowing why.

events.text: Somebody in the Upper Realm has left a little handwritten book on the step where you sign: a register of nothing, naps and herons and soups, every line marked present in a free hand. The last page says: for you, whoever you are now.

choices.text: Read it through

effects.log: You read every line. Nothing in it was paid for. It is the best register you have ever read. You feel, very strongly, that you once helped somebody be able to write it.

choices.text: Add a line of your own

effects.log: You add a line: present, and today's weather. The next morning the book is gone. Somewhere a person who used to flinch at bells, you hope, is reading it and laughing.

events.text: Your sign-in hour finds you in the middle of a duel of honour, blades locked. You feel the System waiting, polite and absurd, like a servant holding tea in a battle.

choices.text: Disengage, sign, and resume

effects.log: You step back, raise a hand, sign in, and step forward again. Your opponent, utterly thrown, loses the next three exchanges. You suspect this will become a story told about you, unfairly.

choices.text: Fight on and let it sign for you

effects.log: You fight on. At the turning of the year, the System signs for you, at your usual place. The duel ends in a draw. The register, you notice, does not care who won.

events.text: It is raining hard at your hour, the kind of rain that fills sandals. Your place is a walk away across mud.

choices.text: Walk through the rain

effects.log: You walk through it. At your place you sign with water running off your chin, and the ding sounds almost amused. You walk home and change. That is the whole story. It is a good one.

choices.text: Sign where you stand, under the eaves

effects.log: You sign under the eaves, on the road, and the run breaks, and you do not mind. The rain on the roof sounds like the register writing many small lines very fast.

events.text: A friend's funeral falls on the day of your sign-in. The mourners are gathered. Your hour comes in the middle of the rites.

choices.text: Step out quietly and sign

effects.log: You step out, sign, and come back in. Nobody notices but the friend's eldest, who later asks where you went. You tell them. They say: that is like our friend. Always somewhere at the same hour.

choices.text: Stay, and let the year be signed for you

effects.log: You stay. The System signs for you at the turning of the year. At the grave you say the friend's name aloud with yours, in your head, present, and feel the register take it.

events.text: A small child of your street has started copying you: every year, at your hour, they march out and stand at the same spot, and say ding, very loudly.

choices.text: Bow to them, host to host

effects.log: You bow, very formally. They bow back. The neighbours laugh. Every year after, until they grow up and move away, there are two of you at the spot, one of whom says ding.

choices.text: Ask what reward they get

effects.log: "A rice cake from grandmother," the child says, "if I do it every year." You think this is the most honest System you have ever heard of, and tell them so.

events.text: A thief has heard that you keep a register that pays out every year, and has broken into your rooms looking for it. They are still there, sitting among your things, utterly baffled, when you come home.

choices.text: Explain there is nothing to steal

effects.log: "It is not a book," you say. "It is the years." The thief looks at you as if you were mad, then sad, then thoughtful. They leave without taking anything. A year later a thief turned porter signs in at the same gate every morning.

choices.text: Detain them, gently

ok.log: You sit them down and give them tea while they wait for the watch. They ask, again and again, where the register is. You tell them it is right here. They never understand.

fail.log: They are quicker than you thought, and gone out of the window with your second-best shoes. You sign in barefoot that year. The ding sounds, if anything, delighted.

events.text: New Year's morning, and your hour. The street is full of children in new clothes bowing to their elders, and you are the eldest anyone here can remember.

choices.text: Sign, then hand out coins

effects.log: You sign, and then sit on your step handing out coins to a queue of bowing children. One asks if you get New Year money too. "Once a year," you say. "From somebody very patient."

choices.text: Sign, and bow to the oldest tree instead

effects.log: You sign, and then bow to the old tree at the end of the street, which was here before you. The children copy you. It becomes, in a few years, a street custom nobody can explain.

events.text: A wandering musician who is blind asks to sit by your place at your hour. They have heard there is a sound there once a year that nobody else can hear, and they want to listen for it.

choices.text: Let them listen

effects.log: They sit beside you. At your hour, you sign. The musician tilts their head, and smiles, and plays one note on their zither, exactly the pitch of your ding. Neither of you says anything.

choices.text: Describe the sound for them

effects.log: You describe it: a small bell in an empty hall, struck by someone careful. The musician writes a song about it. It is played in teahouses for years, and nobody who hums it knows what it is about.

events.text: Your sect, your town, your corner of the murim is at war this year, and your place is on the wrong side of a line of soldiers.

choices.text: Walk through the line at your hour

ok.log: You walk through the line. Nobody quite manages to stop you. You sign, turn, and walk back. Later both armies tell the story, each claiming you as theirs.

fail.log: The line holds. You get a spear-butt in the ribs for your trouble, and the System signs for you at the turning of the year. The war ends the next spring. Your place is still there. (-10 health)

choices.text: Sign where you are, behind the lines

effects.log: You sign where you are. The run breaks. The war ends. You go back to your place the next year and find it untouched, as if waiting.

events.text: You wake with the odd feeling that this year's line has already been written. It has not: the hour has not come. But the System is restless, ringing faintly at nothing.

choices.text: Ask it what is wrong

effects.log: "What is wrong?" A long pause. "Old day," it says. "Bad day. Long ago." You sit with it until your hour, saying nothing, and sign very carefully, and it quiets.

choices.text: Sign early and steady it

effects.log: You go out and sign at your hour, early as it allows, with a firm hand. The ringing settles at once. Some days, you think, even a register needs someone else to be steady.

events.text: A disciple of yours, or a student, or just a young person who follows you about, asks if they can have a System like yours.

choices.text: Give them a notebook and a place

effects.log: You give them a notebook and point to a stone. "Here, once a year," you say. "Write present. I will check." They do it for years. It does not pay them anything. It makes them very strong in a way they cannot explain.

choices.text: Tell them it chose you, not the other way

effects.log: "It chose me," you say. "I only kept coming." They go away and think about it, and, without a System, keep coming. You are prouder of that than of anything the register ever paid.

events.text: You notice, this year, that you can no longer remember a year in which you did not sign. The idea of a blank year has become as strange as a blank sky.

choices.text: Be glad of it

effects.log: You are glad. A life without blanks. Whoever keeps the register would, you think, be glad too. The ding at your hour sounds as if it agrees.

choices.text: Leave one hour unwatched, on purpose

effects.log: You let your hour pass doing nothing at all, to see. At the turning of the year the System signs for you, at your usual place, without a word of reproach. Not a blank, then. Never a blank. You feel looked after.

events.text: An official of the province is counting the households, and asks for your name and your years. You give them. The official frowns at the count, then counts again.

choices.text: Show them your register, line by line

effects.log: You recite your register from the first year: places, years, nothing missing. The official writes it all down and stares. "Our census misses a household in five," they say. "You have missed nothing in your life."

choices.text: Say you have lived a while

effects.log: "I have lived a while," you say. The official writes down a number that will make some future historian very confused, and moves on to the next door.

events.text: The Upper Realm has changed your sign-in. At your hour you kneel on the Jade Stairs and sign, and the System rings like a struck bell, loud enough that every immortal on the stairs stops and turns. In the world below, it never rang like that.

choices.text: Stand and bow to the staring immortals

effects.log: You bow. Most of them bow back, from habit. An old one at the top murmurs, "A sign-in? Here? How very provincial," and is plainly delighted. By evening the whole terrace knows a mortal habit has arrived.

choices.text: Listen to the bell until it fades

effects.log: You listen until it fades. Nobody speaks in it now, and still it sounds close to home, and a little homesick. You look up the endless stair toward where the Archive must be.
